title: The Ethics of Care: Thinking About Relationships, Context, and Responsibility

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Good morning. I'd like to introduce you today to an ethical framework that doesn't fit neatly into the consequentialism-deontology-virtue ethics trio — one that emerged partly as a critique of those frameworks and partly as an attempt to take seriously a dimension of moral life that all three tend to neglect. This is the ethics of care, first systematically developed by psychologist Carol Gilligan in the 1980s and subsequently expanded by philosophers including Nel Noddings and Virginia Held.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: The ethics of care starts from a deceptively simple observation: most moral philosophy has been conducted by people who gave little attention to the moral significance of relationships. The canonical examples of moral dilemmas — the trolley problem, the lying murderer at the door — are typically framed in terms of strangers. But much of the most morally significant territory of human life is relational: parenting, friendship, caregiving, partnership. We are not primarily isolated individuals making abstract decisions; we are deeply embedded in webs of particular relationships that carry particular obligations.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Care ethics holds that attention, responsiveness, and responsibility within relationships are fundamental moral goods — not merely instrumentally important but intrinsically so. The good mother who stays up all night with a sick child is not calculating consequences or applying universal rules; she is responding to the particular needs of a particular child with whom she has a particular relationship. This responsiveness is itself morally significant, and any ethical framework that cannot capture it is missing something important.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Care ethics has several important implications. First, it challenges the idea that impartiality is always a moral virtue. Classical moral philosophy often holds that a good moral agent treats all individuals equally — weighing one person's interests the same as another's, regardless of personal connection. Care ethicists challenge this: partiality towards those we care for — giving your children more attention and resources than strangers' children — is not a moral failing but an expression of a morally fundamental commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Second, care ethics emphasises the importance of context. Moral rules that apply universally may fail to capture what is required in specific relationships and circumstances. What it means to care well for a friend with a serious illness, for a parent with dementia, or for a child with learning difficulties cannot be read off a universal rule — it requires attentiveness to the particular person, knowledge of their history, and the kind of practical judgment that grows from sustained engagement rather than abstract principle.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Third, care ethics challenges the dichotomy between public and private morality. If relational responsibilities are genuinely morally important, then social and political institutions should be designed to support them. The standard liberal view treats care as a private matter — what individuals do within families is largely outside the scope of political ethics. Care ethicists challenge this: institutions that force workers to choose between caring for their children and their economic survival, or that fail to provide support for those caring for elderly or disabled relatives, are making political choices with direct moral consequences.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Andersen
dialogue.text: Critics of care ethics raise several objections. One is that partiality — however natural — can shade into nepotism, tribalism, and the exclusion of those outside our caring relationships. Another is that care ethics, at least in its earlier formulations, was associated with stereotypes about women's "natural" moral orientation — a criticism Gilligan herself later addressed. A third is that care ethics may be better understood as complementing the major frameworks rather than replacing them: it adds something important that they neglect, but does not itself resolve the hardest moral dilemmas. These are real limitations worth taking seriously. But the observation that relationships matter morally — that who you are to someone shapes what you owe them — seems to me undeniably true and philosophically important.

vocab.definition: a preference for or bias towards a particular person or group, especially those one cares about
vocab.example: "Care ethics holds that partiality towards those we love is not a failing but a moral commitment."

vocab.definition: the quality of treating all parties and individuals equally, without favouritism
vocab.example: "Classical moral philosophy often holds that impartiality is a moral virtue."

vocab.definition: the quality of paying careful attention to others' needs and experiences
vocab.example: "Care ethics prizes attentiveness — really noticing what the particular person in your care needs."
